subject: Cognitive Science
title: Categorization Under Pressure
description: A micro-lesson that makes Categorization Under Pressure usable.

hook.text: A doctor in the ER has seconds to classify symptoms. Fast categorization can save a life.

buildup.text: Under time pressure, people rely more on surface similarity and less on deep causal reasoning.

discovery.text: Rushed participants classify a bat as a bird more often—it looks and flies like one.

twist.text: Experts resist this shift. Trained radiologists still spot rare patterns under stress.

climax.text: Deep knowledge makes categorization automatic, freeing it from time pressure's distortions.

punchline.text: Hurry makes you think in shortcuts.

quiz.question: How does time pressure affect categorization?
options: People rely more on surface similarity

details.summary: Under time pressure, stress, or cognitive load, people shift toward simpler categorization strategies. They rely more heavily on prototypes, use fewer features, and default to broad stereotypes. This shows that category use is flexible but degrades when cognitive resources are depleted.
details.whyItMatters: Real-world decisions are often made under pressure. Knowing that categorization simplifies under stress explains snap judgments, errors, and stereotype reliance in high-stakes situations.
takeaways: Stress and time pressure simplify categorization strategies
People rely more on prototypes when resources are limited
Stereotype use increases under cognitive load

faq.question: Why does stress increase stereotype use?
faq.answer: Stereotypes are cognitively cheap. They require no deliberation and provide instant categorization. When working memory is loaded by stress or multitasking, the brain defaults to these efficient shortcuts. Controlled, individuating processing requires resources that stress depletes.

faq.question: Can training reduce categorization errors under pressure?
faq.answer: Partially. Extensive practice makes more nuanced categorization more automatic, reducing reliance on stereotypes even under load. Police and medical training aim for this. However, extreme stress can still push even trained professionals toward simpler categorical thinking.
